analysis.one_liner: Restores state and local power to regulate cable TV rates and requires cable systems to carry local broadcast channels.
analysis.headline: Backed by 35 House members from both parties and the subject of four subcommittee hearings, the bill never got a floor vote and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 1984 law barred most states and cities from regulating cable prices, cable bills rose far faster than inflation while customers faced regional monopolies. This bill would have repealed those limits, letting state and local regulators review and change cable rates, block media companies from controlling local cable systems, and require cable systems to keep carrying local broadcast stations on their basic tier. It never came out of committee for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, who would gain a local regulator they could petition when rates rose or service tiers were reshuffled. Local broadcast stations, which would be guaranteed a spot on cable's basic tier. State and local franchising authorities, which would regain the power to review rates within 60 days of a hearing and to weigh ownership concentration when granting or renewing franchises.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the 1984 limits on state and local authority to regulate cable rates, and lets regulators require rate changes after a cable operator alters its service, such as rearranging tiers, with a final decision due within 60 days of public notice and a hearing.
The bill's findings state that in 1988 cable rates rose 10.6% nationally while overall inflation was 4.4%, and that the 1984 deregulation law had created regional cable monopolies.
The bill would let state or local franchising authorities bar a person from owning a cable system because of ownership of other mass media, enforced through franchise renewal and transfer decisions.

It would require cable systems to carry local broadcast station signals on the basic tier, at the channel where each station was carried in 1985 or a channel acceptable to the station, as a condition of the compulsory copyright license, with no expiration date.

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, who would lose the price and service-tier freedom they held under the 1984 law, face mandated carriage of broadcast stations on their basic tier, and could be blocked from owning local cable systems where they controlled other media.

drawbacks.text: Rate regulation can discourage investment in cable systems and slow network upgrades, the main argument behind the 1984 law's deregulation of the industry.
Mandated carriage of broadcast stations on the basic tier takes up cable channel space, which can crowd out newer or specialized programming and reduce viewer choice.
The 60-day deadline for a final rate decision after public notice could pressure regulators into rushed rulings on complex pricing questions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households facing cable bills rising at more than double the inflation rate under regional monopolies, restored local rate review is a real, tangible benefit. The costs are real but narrower: some risk to system investment, some channel space given to broadcast stations, and a tight regulatory clock. On balance this is a modest, targeted consumer protection rather than a sweeping takeover of the industry.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, got four subcommittee hearings in 1990, and was never reported out for a House vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced May 3, 1989 by Rep. Christopher Shays and referred jointly to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees.
In May 1989 it was sent to the Telecommunications and Finance Subcommittee and the Courts, Intellectual Property, and Administration of Justice Subcommittee.
The subcommittees held hearings on March 1, April 19, May 9, and May 16, 1990, but the full committees never took it up and the House never voted on it.
By April 1990 the bill had drawn 34 cosponsors from both parties, 25 Democrats and 9 Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators came out ahead: they kept the freedom from state and local rate regulation won under the 1984 law, while subscribers continued paying unregulated rates in monopoly markets.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 29 additional sponsors over the following year.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the rest of the Congress, referring it to a subcommittee that held hearings but never reporting it to the floor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee that held hearings but never reported it to the floor.

against.name: Cable television industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed restoring state and local rate regulation during the cable re-regulation debate of this era.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan: 25 of 257 House Democrats and 9 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored, with a Republican lead sponsor, but the bill never reached a floor vote where partisan splits could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their 1984-era exemption from state and local rate regulation, required rate changes after service changes, and imposed must-carry and ownership limits. Operators had raised rates far faster than inflation as regional monopolies, so their gain came directly at subscribers' expense.
The bill ties the cable compulsory copyright license to must-carry rules, guaranteeing broadcast stations a place on cable's basic tier at their chosen channel, with no expiration date.
Companies owning other mass media could be barred from owning local cable systems under franchise renewal and transfer decisions.
